ety.text: From Middle English at, from Old English æt (“at, near, by, toward”), from Proto-West Germanic *at, from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, near, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”). Cognate with Scots at (“at”), North Frisian äät, äit, et, it (“at”), Danish at (“to”), Swedish åt (“for, toward”), Norwegian åt (“to”), Faroese at (“at, to, toward”), Icelandic að (“to, towards”), Gothic 𐌰𐍄 (at, “at”), Latin ad (“to, near”).

senses.d: In, near, or in the general vicinity of (a particular place).
ex: A climate treaty was signed at Kyoto in 1997.
She's at Oxford University, studying chemistry.

senses.d: Working for (a company) or in (a place or situation).
ex: He used to be at Lehman Brothers. Now he's at Merrill Lynch.
'Where does he work?' — 'I think he's still at the solicitors.'

senses.d: Indicating distance or direction relative to the speaker.
ex: Target at five miles. Prepare torpedoes.
Look out! UFO at two o'clock!

senses.d: Present or taking place during (an event).
ex: There was a big fight at the class reunion.

senses.d: Indicating time of occurrence, especially an instant of time, or a period of time relatively short in context or from the speaker’s perspective.
ex: at six o’clock; at dawn; at closing time; at the age of twelve; at night; at the moment
Hi, Anne. Are you busy? — Hi, Anna. Yes. At 10 a.m. I am writing.

senses.d: (also as at; before dates) On (a particular date).
In the direction of; towards; (often implied to be in a hostile or careless manner).
ex: Don’t just talk at someone; really listen to what they have to say.
Stones were thrown at us, but we couldn't see who did.

senses.d: Indicating action bearing upon something, especially continued or repeated action.
ex: My cat keeps scratching at the furniture.
At my request, they agreed to move us to another hotel.
He jumped at the sudden noise.
